**International Copper Study Group Environmental and Economic Committee Twenty Seventh Regular Meeting 6 October 2009, 10:45 a.m. – 1.00 p.m. Lisbon, orP tugal Copper Scrap Researc Pro ect: Octoh j ber 2009 Report Summary** 

### **ICSG/EEC/27/3** 

**1. Copper Scrap Research Project Structure.** In October 2007, ICSG member countries approved the project proposal, giving a priority to the improvement of ICSG copper scrap statistics, data analysis on China, India and Russia copper scrap markets, information of copper scrap trade barriers and incentives to recycling and bibliographic research on copper scrap related **issues** . **The original requested studies where approved by members in April 2009** , **nevertheless** , **2008 findings revealed the** need to obtain more primary data, analysis and estimations on domestic scrap generation, use and trade in China, Japan and the Rest of the World. Funds where approved for additional research in April 2009. **2. Advances in Secretariat Research.** Between May and October 2009 the Secretariat contracted the external work and advanced in house with the analysis of copper content of global trade flows. World scrap generation in global waste electric **and electronic equipment was estimated using as a base the findings of the European Commission reports** . **A commercial** analysis of the trade value of the main global copper scrap flows was also completed by the Secretariat. The Secretariat deepened the study of the role of scrap in the Chinese copper market expanding scrap price data collection and analysis of the market based in copper scrap spreads. The study of the first use of copper scrap in Chinese copper/alloy semis manufacturing industry was deepened. The Secretariat requested improvements to first drafts of the survey of semis and smelters in China and to the domestic generation reports. Finally we compared recent findings on China copper scrap market with ICSG data and with other sources **,** and **p** re **p** ared the **Executive Summary (** Pa **g** e 6 **)** includin **g** ke **y** findin **g** s of this ste **p** s and recommendations for future work. 

**3. Advances in Outsourced Work.** The generous contribution of the Japanese industry to this project, through **MERIJ** complete ‐ updated research including domestic recycling in 2001 2008, updated copper flows in Japan and a deep analysis of their trade flows to China is the most recent outcome. Our outsourced work in China on May ‐ October 2009 with **BGRIMM** produced some fruits included in this re **p** ort **,** in **p** articular domestic scra **p g** eneration estimations and forecasts. A final re **p** ort will be available in . Also new primary data on copper scrap use in semis and smelters at the plant level in China for the last 10 years including 2009 plans was obtained using a plant survey. United States based **Nathan Inc.** work produced a master database of copper and copper alloys producers outside of Japan, Russia

, India and China (Ex ‐ JRIC). Based in ICSG 847 plants, the consultants found 273 new plants and now a database of 1120 semis with contacts is available for ex ‐ JRIC countries. The survey targeting the 1120 semis was launched in September 2009 and first draft is expected for November 2009. **4. Next Step and Actions from Member Countries** . . If member countries do not request additional research in the October 2009, ongoing outsourced work in Japan, China, United States, same as Secretariat research will end in January 2010. A draft final report, including most relevant findings and a research agenda beyond the project will be delivered by April 2010 as planned originally. As our Copper Scrap Survey in China 2009 is of public interest if published this year, member countries are ‐ invited to approve its publication and sale in Q4 09. Member countries are also requested to give approval for the Secretariat to consider the engagement of external consultants to review and provide feedback on draft advances of the Copper Scrap Project Fina **l** Report. - Copper scrap is a concept that hides many different metals and end of life products containing copper. - **The % of copper and other contents in copper scrap** makes hard to reconcile national statistics on international scrap trade. Global copper scrap markets are more competitive and transparent than the common perception as prices are competitive and there are many supplyers and users. - Access to scrap use data in semis and smelters is significantly less transparent in some cases than the scrap market itself. In consequence ICSG and its members should consider strategies to increase transparency at the base: more updated country level first use data of copper/alloy fabricators production. - Even when in some western countries scrap market prices are easy to follow, to obtain data on scrap use from statistical bodies and industry asociations is challenging in some cases. Nevertheless we found a proactive attitude to exchange data and information when we surveyed large Chinese semis. Secondary **smelters shared use and production data but not** prices paid for their old scrap. - **Global copper scrap export supply is concentrated : 48% from top 5 exporters.
